title: Why a Promise always beats setTimeout(0) in JavaScript
description:
A zero millisecond setTimeout still runs after every line of synchronous code, and a Promise callback jumps ahead of it every time. This Short walks through the event loop's three lanes: sync code on the call stack, then the microtask queue, then the task queue. Once you can see those lanes, async JavaScript stops feeling like magic.

Source lesson(s):
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/javascript-mastery-path/level-2/03-async-javascript-i/

#Shorts

beats.narration: This line has a zero millisecond timeout. So it fires immediately, right? Nope. It runs dead last, after every other line.
JavaScript runs all the synchronous code first. That timeout callback has to wait for the call stack to empty, even when the delay is zero.

Add a promise and it gets stranger. The promise callback cuts ahead of the timeout. Promise callbacks go in the microtask queue, and the event loop fully drains that before it touches a single setTimeout.

display.output:
1: sync start
2: sync end
3: promise (microtask queue)
4: setTimeout (task queue)

beats.narration: So the real order is: all sync code, then every microtask, then the next task. Once you see those three lanes, the event loop stops feeling like magic.
